title: One attempt, one verifier
lesson: Keep each OAuth sign-in's verifier bound to its authorization attempt: the token endpoint rejects a code paired with another attempt's verifier.
limitations: Illustrative concurrent sign-ins in an agent host; A–D represent full random verifier values, not literal secrets.
Consent, TLS and other OAuth validation are omitted. A matching verifier does not by itself guarantee token issuance.
PKCE does not enforce agent permissions or turn persistent prompts into access controls.

Audio was decoded and analysed for levels and activity near declared cues, with spectrogram inspection; it was not physically heard. Perceptual quality and exact audiovisual synchronization remain untested.

Original author evidence is retained separately; final encoded evidence and independent comparison are in reviews/comparisons/oauth-pkce/. No live provider test or continuous real-time playback review was performed.

transcript.text: An agent host starts sign-in A. It keeps a fresh secret called a verifier and sends an S256 challenge derived from it. The authorization server associates that challenge with code A and returns the code.

The host sends code A and verifier A to the token endpoint. The server transforms the verifier and finds the stored challenge matches. Assuming the other OAuth checks pass, it issues a token and consumes the code.
Two new sign-ins, B and C, overlap. Each has a separate verifier, challenge and code. Their values belong to separate authorization attempts.

An illustrative client bug puts C's verifier into B's exchange. The server receives code B with verifier C. Its transformed value differs from B's stored challenge, so the server returns invalid_grant and issues no token.

The host clears the failed flow and starts fresh sign-in D with its own verifier. D's challenge and code remain paired through exchange. The comparison matches and the valid request receives a token. This protects the code exchange; agent permissions still require separate access controls.

corrections: Rename the OAuth client to Agent host, matching the chapter scenario and distinguishing it from the protected tool service.
